# cranelift_control - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-control/^0.133.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cranelift-control)Cranelift Control

This is the home of the control plane of chaos mode, a compilation feature
intended to be turned on for certain fuzz targets. When the feature is
turned off, as is normally the case, [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) will be a zero-sized
type and optimized away.

While the feature is turned on, the struct [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)
provides functionality to tap into pseudo-randomness at specific locations
in the code. It may be used for targeted fuzzing of compiler internals,
e.g. manipulate heuristic optimizations, clobber undefined register bits
etc.

There are two ways to acquire a [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html):

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary)for the real deal (requires the- `fuzz`feature, enabled by default)
- [default](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.default)for an “empty” control plane which always returns default values

[§](https://docs.rs#fuel-limit)Fuel Limit

Controls the number of mutations or optimizations that the compiler will perform before stopping.

When a perturbation introduced by chaos mode triggers a bug, it may not be immediately clear which of the introduced perturbations was the trigger. The fuel limit can then be used to binary-search for the trigger. It limits the number of perturbations introduced by the control plane. The fuel limit will typically be set with a command line argument passed to a fuzz target. For example:

`cargo fuzz run --features chaos $TARGET -- --fuel=16`[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-support)`no_std` support

This crate compiles in `no_std` environments, although both the `fuzz`
or `chaos` features have a dependency on `std`. This means that on `no_std`
you can’t use [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary) to initialize [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) and can’t enable
chaos mode, although the rest of the usual [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) API is available.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)- Plane
- A shim for ControlPlane when chaos mode is disabled.
Please see the [crate-level documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html).

---

# cranelift_entity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/^0.133.0/

## Expand description

Array-based data structures using densely numbered entity references as mapping keys.

This crate defines a number of data structures based on arrays. The arrays are not indexed by
`usize` as usual, but by *entity references* which are integers wrapped in new-types. This has
a couple advantages:

- Improved type safety. The various map and set types accept a specific key type, so there is no confusion about the meaning of an array index, as there is with plain arrays.
- Smaller indexes. The normal `usize`index is often 64 bits which is way too large for most purposes. The entity reference types can be smaller, allowing for more compact data structures.

The `EntityRef` trait should be implemented by types to be used as indexed. The `entity_impl!`
macro provides convenient defaults for types wrapping `u32` which is common.

- `PrimaryMap`
- `SecondaryMap`
- `SparseMap`
- `EntitySet`
- `EntityList`- `Vec`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [packed_](https://docs.rs/packed_option/index.html)- option
- Compact representation of `Option<T>`for types with a reserved value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [entity_](https://docs.rs/macro.entity_impl.html)- impl
- Macro which provides the common implementation of a 32-bit entity reference.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Boxed](https://docs.rs/struct.BoxedSlice.html)- Slice
- A slice mapping `K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/struct.EntityList.html)- List
- A small list of entity references allocated from a pool.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/struct.EntitySet.html)- Set
- A set of `K`for densely indexed entity references.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.IterEntityRange.html)- Entity - Range
- Iterator type returned by `iter_entity_range`.
- [IterMut](https://docs.rs/struct.IterMut.html)
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [Keys](https://docs.rs/struct.Keys.html)
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListPool.html)- Pool
- A memory pool for storing lists of `T`.
- [Primary](https://docs.rs/struct.PrimaryMap.html)- Map
- A primary mapping `K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- [Secondary](https://docs.rs/struct.SecondaryMap.html)- Map
- A mapping `K -> V`for densely indexed entity references.
- [SetIter](https://docs.rs/struct.SetIter.html)
- An iterator over the elements in an `EntitySet`.
- [Sparse](https://docs.rs/struct.SparseMap.html)- Map
- A sparse mapping of entity references.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Entity](https://docs.rs/trait.EntityRef.html)- Ref
- A type wrapping a small integer index should implement `EntityRef`so it can be used as the key of an`SecondaryMap`or`SparseMap`.
- [Sparse](https://docs.rs/trait.SparseMapValue.html)- MapValue
- Trait for extracting keys from values stored in a `SparseMap`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Iterate over a `Range<E: EntityRef>`, yielding a sequence of`E`items.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Sparse](https://docs.rs/type.SparseSet.html)- Set
- A sparse set of entity references.

# hashbrown - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hashbrown/^0.17/

## Expand description

This crate is a Rust port of Google’s high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash
map, adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust’s standard `HashMap`
and `HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_map/index.html)- map
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_set/index.html)- set
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_table/index.html)- table
- A hash table implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHashBuilder.html)- Hash - Builder
- Default hash builder for the `S`type parameter of`HashMap``HashSet`
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHasher.html)- Hasher
- Default hasher for `HashMap``HashSet`
- [HashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.HashMap.html)
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [HashSet](https://docs.rs/struct.HashSet.html)
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/struct.HashTable.html)- Table
- Low-level hash table with explicit hashing.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [TryReserve](https://docs.rs/enum.TryReserveError.html)- Error
- The error type for `try_reserve`methods.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Equivalent](https://docs.rs/trait.Equivalent.html)
- Key equivalence trait.

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4.28/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# postcard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/postcard/^1.1.3/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#postcard)Postcard

Postcard is a `#![no_std]` focused serializer and deserializer for Serde.

Postcard aims to be convenient for developers in constrained environments, while allowing for flexibility to customize behavior as needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-goals)Design Goals

- Design primarily for `#![no_std]`usage, in embedded or other constrained contexts
- Support a maximal set of `serde`features, so`postcard`can be used as a drop in replacement
- Avoid special differences in code between communication code written for a microcontroller or a desktop/server PC
- Be resource efficient - memory usage, code size, developer time, and CPU time; in that order
- Allow library users to customize the serialization and deserialization behavior to fit their bespoke needs

[§](https://docs.rs#format-stability)Format Stability

As of v1.0.0, `postcard` has a documented and stable wire format. More information about this
wire format can be found in the `spec/` folder of the Postcard repository, or viewed online
at [https://postcard.jamesmunns.com](https://postcard.jamesmunns.com).

Work towards the Postcard Specification and portions of the Postcard 1.0 Release were sponsored by Mozilla Corporation.

[§](https://docs.rs#variable-length-data)Variable Length Data

All signed and unsigned integers larger than eight bits are encoded using a [Varint](https://postcard.jamesmunns.com/wire-format.html#varint-encoded-integers).
This includes the length of array slices, as well as the discriminant of `enums`.

For more information, see the [Varint](https://postcard.jamesmunns.com/wire-format.html#varint-encoded-integers) chapter of the wire specification.

[§](https://docs.rs#example---serializationdeserialization)Example - Serialization/Deserialization

Postcard can serialize and deserialize messages similar to other `serde` formats.

Using the default `heapless` feature to serialize to a `heapless::Vec<u8>`:

```
use core::ops::Deref;
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
use postcard::{from_bytes, to_vec};
use heapless::Vec;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
struct RefStruct<'a> {
    bytes: &'a [u8],
    str_s: &'a str,
}
let message = "hElLo";
let bytes = [0x01, 0x10, 0x02, 0x20];
let output: Vec<u8, 11> = to_vec(&RefStruct {
    bytes: &bytes,
    str_s: message,
}).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    &[0x04, 0x01, 0x10, 0x02, 0x20, 0x05, b'h', b'E', b'l', b'L', b'o',],
    output.deref()
);
let out: RefStruct = from_bytes(output.deref()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    out,
    RefStruct {
        bytes: &bytes,
        str_s: message,
    }
);
```
Or the optional `alloc` feature to serialize to an `alloc::vec::Vec<u8>`:

```
use core::ops::Deref;
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
use postcard::{from_bytes, to_allocvec};
extern crate alloc;
use alloc::vec::Vec;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
struct RefStruct<'a> {
    bytes: &'a [u8],
    str_s: &'a str,
}
let message = "hElLo";
let bytes = [0x01, 0x10, 0x02, 0x20];
let output: Vec<u8> = to_allocvec(&RefStruct {
    bytes: &bytes,
    str_s: message,
}).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    &[0x04, 0x01, 0x10, 0x02, 0x20, 0x05, b'h', b'E', b'l', b'L', b'o',],
    output.deref()
);
let out: RefStruct = from_bytes(output.deref()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    out,
    RefStruct {
        bytes: &bytes,
        str_s: message,
    }
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#flavors)Flavors

`postcard` supports a system called `Flavors`, which are used to modify the way
postcard serializes or processes serialized data. These flavors act as “plugins” or “middlewares”
during the serialization or deserialization process, and can be combined to obtain complex protocol formats.

See the documentation of the `ser_flavors` or `de_flavors` modules for more information on usage.

[§](https://docs.rs#setup---cargotoml)Setup - `Cargo.toml`

Don’t forget to add [the  no-std subset](https://serde.rs/no-std.html) of

`serde` along with `postcard` to the `[dependencies]` section of your `Cargo.toml`!```
[dependencies]
postcard = "1.0.0"
# By default, `serde` has the `std` feature enabled, which makes it unsuitable for embedded targets
# disabling default-features fixes this
serde = { version = "1.0.*", default-features = false }
```

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes.html)- bytes
- Deserialize a message of type `T`from a byte slice. The unused portion (if any) of the byte slice is not returned.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes_cobs.html)- bytes_ - cobs
- Deserialize a message of type `T`from a cobs-encoded byte slice.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes_crc32.html)- bytes_ - crc32 - `use-crc`
- Conveniently deserialize a message of type `T`from a byte slice with a Crc. The unused portion (if any) of the byte slice is not returned.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_eio.html)- eio - `embedded-io-04`or- `embedded-io-06`
- Deserialize a message of type `T`from a`embedded_io``Read`
- [from_io](https://docs.rs/fn.from_io.html)- `use-std`
- Deserialize a message of type `T`from a`std::io::Read`
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize_with_flavor.html)- with_ - flavor
- `serialize_with_flavor()`has three generic parameters,- `T, F, O`.
- [take_](https://docs.rs/fn.take_from_bytes.html)- from_ - bytes
- Deserialize a message of type `T`from a byte slice. The unused portion (if any) of the byte slice is returned for further usage
- [take_](https://docs.rs/fn.take_from_bytes_cobs.html)- from_ - bytes_ - cobs
- Deserialize a message of type `T`from a cobs-encoded byte slice.
- [take_](https://docs.rs/fn.take_from_bytes_crc32.html)- from_ - bytes_ - crc32 - `use-crc`
- Conveniently deserialize a message of type `T`from a byte slice with a Crc. The unused portion (if any) of the byte slice is returned for further usage
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_allocvec.html)- allocvec - `alloc`
- Serialize a `T`to an`alloc::vec::Vec<u8>`.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_allocvec_cobs.html)- allocvec_ - cobs - `alloc`
- Serialize and COBS encode a `T`to an`alloc::vec::Vec<u8>`.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_allocvec_crc32.html)- allocvec_ - crc32 - `alloc`and- `use-crc`
- Conveniently serialize a `T`to a`heapless::Vec<u8>`, with the`Vec`containing data followed by a 32-bit CRC. The CRC bytes are included in the output`Vec`.
- [to_eio](https://docs.rs/fn.to_eio.html)- `embedded-io-04`or- `embedded-io-06`
- Serialize a `T`to an`embedded_io Write`

- Conveniently serialize a `T`to a`heapless::Vec<u8>`, with the`Vec`containing data followed by a 32-bit CRC. The CRC bytes are included in the output`Vec`.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.228/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# sha2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sha2/^0.10.2/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [SHA-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2) cryptographic hash algorithms.

There are 6 standard algorithms specified in the SHA-2 standard: [ Sha224](https://docs.rs/type.Sha224.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha256.html)

`Sha256`[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_224.html)

`Sha512_224`[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_256.html)

`Sha512_256`[, and](https://docs.rs/type.Sha384.html)

`Sha384`[.](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512.html)

`Sha512`Algorithmically, there are only 2 core algorithms: SHA-256 and SHA-512. All other algorithms are just applications of these with different initial hash values, and truncated to different digest bit lengths. The first two algorithms in the list are based on SHA-256, while the last four are based on SHA-512.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#one-shot-api)One-shot API

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha2::{Sha256, Digest};
let result = Sha256::digest(b"hello world");
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    b94d27b9934d3e08a52e52d7da7dabfac484efe37a5380ee9088f7ace2efcde9
")[..]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#incremental-api)Incremental API

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha2::{Sha256, Sha512, Digest};
// create a Sha256 object
let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
// write input message
hasher.update(b"hello world");
// read hash digest and consume hasher
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    b94d27b9934d3e08a52e52d7da7dabfac484efe37a5380ee9088f7ace2efcde9
")[..]);
// same for Sha512
let mut hasher = Sha512::new();
hasher.update(b"hello world");
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    309ecc489c12d6eb4cc40f50c902f2b4d0ed77ee511a7c7a9bcd3ca86d4cd86f
    989dd35bc5ff499670da34255b45b0cfd830e81f605dcf7dc5542e93ae9cd76f
")[..]);
```
Also see [RustCrypto/hashes](https://github.com/RustCrypto/hashes) readme.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [digest](https://docs.rs/digest/0.10.7/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/digest/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Sha256](https://docs.rs/struct.Sha256VarCore.html)- VarCore
- Core block-level SHA-256 hasher with variable output size.
- [Sha512](https://docs.rs/struct.Sha512VarCore.html)- VarCore
- Core block-level SHA-512 hasher with variable output size.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Digest](https://docs.rs/trait.Digest.html)
- Convenience wrapper trait covering functionality of cryptographic hash functions with fixed output size.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [compress256](https://docs.rs/fn.compress256.html)- `compress`
- Raw SHA-256 compression function.
- [compress512](https://docs.rs/fn.compress512.html)- `compress`
- Raw SHA-512 compression function.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Sha224](https://docs.rs/type.Sha224.html)
- SHA-224 hasher.
- [Sha256](https://docs.rs/type.Sha256.html)
- SHA-256 hasher.
- [Sha384](https://docs.rs/type.Sha384.html)
- SHA-384 hasher.

- SHA-512 hasher.

- SHA-512/224 hasher.
- [Sha512_](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_256.html)- 256
- SHA-512/256 hasher.

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).# rust-smallvec

"Small vector" optimization for Rust: store up to a small number of items on the stack

## Example

```
use ;

// This SmallVec can hold up to 4 items on the stack:
let mut v:  = smallvec!;
// It will automatically move its contents to the heap if
// contains more than four items:
v.push;
// SmallVec points to a slice, so you can use normal slice
// indexing and other methods to access its contents:
v = v + v;
v.sort;
```

# souper_ir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/souper-ir/^2.1.0/

## Expand description

A library for manipulating [Souper](https://github.com/google/souper) IR.

This crate provides AST types for parsing or generating Souper IR. It is a suitable building block either for writing a custom LHS extractor, or for translating learned optimizations into your own peephole optimizations pass.

[§](https://docs.rs#ast)AST

The AST type definitions and builders live in the `souper_ir::ast` module.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-souper-ir)Parsing Souper IR

When the `parse` Cargo feature is enabled, the `souper_ir::parse` module
contains functions for parsing Souper IR from a file or an in-memory string.

```
use std::path::Path;
// We provide a filename to get better error messages.
let filename = Path::new("example.souper");
let replacements = souper_ir::parse::parse_replacements_str("
    ;; x + x --> 2 * x
    %0 = var
    %1 = add %0, %0
    %2 = mul %0, 2
    cand %1, %2
    ;; x & x --> x
    %0 = var
    %1 = and %0, %0
    cand %1, %0
", Some(filename))?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#emitting-souper-irs-text-format)Emitting Souper IR’s Text Format

When the `stringify` Cargo feature is enabled, then the
`souper_ir::ast::Replacement`, `souper_ir::ast::LeftHandSide`, and
`souper_ir::ast::RightHandSide` types all implement `std::fmt::Display`. The
`Display` implementation writes the AST type out as Souper’s text format.

```
use souper_ir::ast;
// Build this Souper left-hand side:
//
//     %x:i32 = var
//     %y = mul %x, 2
//     infer %y
//
// We expect that Souper would be able to synthesize a right-hand side that
// does a left shift by one instead of a multiplication.
let mut lhs = ast::LeftHandSideBuilder::default();
let x = lhs.assignment(
    Some("x".into()),
    Some(ast::Type { width: 32 }),
    ast::AssignmentRhs::Var,
    vec![],
);
let y = lhs.assignment(
    Some("y".into()),
    None,
    ast::Instruction::Mul {
        a: x.into(),
        b: ast::Constant { value: 2, r#type: None }.into(),
    },
    vec![],
);
let lhs = lhs.finish(y, vec![]);
// Now we can stringify the LHS (and then, presumably, give it to Souper)
// with `std::fmt::Display`:
use std::io::Write;
let mut file = std::fs::File::create("my-lhs.souper")?;
write!(&mut file, "{}", lhs)?;
```

# criterion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/criterion/^0.8.2/

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

See
[the user guide](https://criterion-rs.github.io/book/index.html)
for examples as well as details on the measurement and analysis process,
and the output.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features:

- Collects detailed statistics, providing strong confidence that changes to performance are real, not measurement noise.
- Produces detailed charts, providing thorough understanding of your code’s performance behavior.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_executor/index.html)- executor
- This module defines a trait that can be used to plug in different Futures executors into Criterion.rs’ async benchmarking support.
- [measurement](https://docs.rs/measurement/index.html)
- This module defines a set of traits that can be used to plug different measurements (eg.
Unix’s Processor Time, CPU or GPU performance counters, etc.) into Criterion.rs. It also
includes the `WallTime`
- [profiler](https://docs.rs/profiler/index.html)
- This module provides an extension trait which allows in-process profilers
to be hooked into the `--profile-time`argument at compile-time. Users of out-of-process profilers such as perf don’t need to do anything special.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_group.html)- group
- Macro used to define a function group for the benchmark harness; see the
`criterion_main!`
- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_main.html)- main
- Macro which expands to a benchmark harness.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncBencher.html)- Bencher
- Async/await variant of `Bencher`
- [Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html)
- Timer struct used to iterate a benchmarked function and measure the runtime.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkGroup.html)- Group
- Structure used to group together a set of related benchmarks, along with custom configuration settings for groups of benchmarks. All benchmarks performed using a benchmark group will be grouped together in the final report.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkId.html)- Id
- Simple structure representing an ID for a benchmark. The ID must be unique within a benchmark group.
- [Criterion](https://docs.rs/struct.Criterion.html)
- The benchmark manager
- [Plot](https://docs.rs/struct.PlotConfiguration.html)- Configuration
- Contains the configuration options for the plots generated by a particular benchmark or benchmark group.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Axis](https://docs.rs/enum.AxisScale.html)- Scale
- Axis scaling type. Specified via `PlotConfiguration::summary_scale`
- [Baseline](https://docs.rs/enum.Baseline.html)
- Baseline describes how the `baseline_directory`is handled.
- [Batch](https://docs.rs/enum.BatchSize.html)- Size
- Argument to `Bencher::iter_batched``Bencher::iter_batched_ref`
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/enum.BenchmarkFilter.html)- Filter
- Benchmark filtering support.
- [Plotting](https://docs.rs/enum.PlottingBackend.html)- Backend
- Enum used to select the plotting backend.
- [Sampling](https://docs.rs/enum.SamplingMode.html)- Mode
- This enum allows the user to control how Criterion.rs chooses the iteration count when sampling.
The default is `Auto`, which will choose a method automatically based on the iteration time during the warm-up phase.
- [Throughput](https://docs.rs/enum.Throughput.html)
- Enum representing different ways of measuring the throughput of benchmarked code. If the throughput setting is configured for a benchmark then the estimated throughput will be reported as well as the time per iteration.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [black_](https://docs.rs/fn.black_box.html)- box - Deprecated
- A function that is opaque to the optimizer, used to prevent the compiler from optimizing away computations in a benchmark.

# env_logger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/env_logger/^0.11.5/

## Expand description

A simple logger that can be configured via environment variables, for use
with the logging facade exposed by the [ log crate](https://docs.rs/log).

Despite having “env” in its name, ** env_logger** can also be configured by
other means besides environment variables. See

[the examples](https://github.com/rust-cli/env_logger/tree/main/examples)in the source repository for more approaches.

By default, `env_logger` writes logs to `stderr`, but can be configured to
instead write them to `stdout`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use log::{debug, error, log_enabled, info, Level};
env_logger::init();
debug!("this is a debug {}", "message");
error!("this is printed by default");
if log_enabled!(Level::Info) {
    let x = 3 * 4; // expensive computation
    info!("the answer was: {}", x);
}
```
Assumes the binary is `main`:

```
$ RUST_LOG=error ./main
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z ERROR main] this is printed by default
```
```
$ RUST_LOG=info ./main
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z ERROR main] this is printed by default
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z INFO main] the answer was: 12
```
```
$ RUST_LOG=debug ./main
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z DEBUG main] this is a debug message
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z ERROR main] this is printed by default
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z INFO main] the answer was: 12
```
You can also set the log level on a per module basis:

```
$ RUST_LOG=main=info ./main
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z ERROR main] this is printed by default
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z INFO main] the answer was: 12
```
And enable all logging:

```
$ RUST_LOG=main ./main
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z DEBUG main] this is a debug message
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z ERROR main] this is printed by default
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z INFO main] the answer was: 12
```
If the binary name contains hyphens, you will need to replace them with underscores:

```
$ RUST_LOG=my_app ./my-app
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z DEBUG my_app] this is a debug message
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z ERROR my_app] this is printed by default
[2017-11-09T02:12:24Z INFO my_app] the answer was: 12
```
This is because Rust modules and crates cannot contain hyphens
in their name, although `cargo` continues to accept them.

See the documentation for the [ log crate](https://docs.rs/log) for more
information about its API.

[§](https://docs.rs#enabling-logging)Enabling logging

**By default all logging is disabled except for the  error level**

The ** RUST_LOG** environment variable controls logging with the syntax:

`RUST_LOG=[target][=][level][,...]`Or in other words, its a comma-separated list of directives.
Directives can filter by **target**, by **level**, or both (using `=`).

For example,

`RUST_LOG=data=debug,hardware=debug`**target** is typically the path of the module the message
in question originated from, though it can be overridden.
The path is rooted in the name of the crate it was compiled for, so if
your program is in a file called, for example, `hello.rs`, the path would
simply be `hello`.

Furthermore, the log can be filtered using prefix-search based on the specified log target.

For example, `RUST_LOG=example` would match the following targets:

- `example`
- `example::test`
- `example::test::module::submodule`
- `examples::and_more_examples`

When providing the crate name or a module path, explicitly specifying the log level is optional. If omitted, all logging for the item will be enabled.

**level** is the maximum [ log::Level](https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/enum.Level.html) to be shown and includes:

- `error`
- `warn`
- `info`
- `debug`
- `trace`
- `off`(pseudo level to disable all logging for the target)

Logging level names are case-insensitive; e.g.,
`debug`, `DEBUG`, and `dEbuG` all represent the same logging level. For
consistency, our convention is to use the lower case names. Where our docs
do use other forms, they do so in the context of specific examples, so you
won’t be surprised if you see similar usage in the wild.

Some examples of valid values of `RUST_LOG` are:

- `RUST_LOG=hello`turns on all logging for the- `hello`module
- `RUST_LOG=trace`turns on all logging for the application, regardless of its name
- `RUST_LOG=TRACE`turns on all logging for the application, regardless of its name (same as previous)
- `RUST_LOG=info`turns on all info logging
- `RUST_LOG=INFO`turns on all info logging (same as previous)
- `RUST_LOG=hello=debug`turns on debug logging for- `hello`
- `RUST_LOG=hello=DEBUG`turns on debug logging for- `hello`(same as previous)
- `RUST_LOG=hello,std::option`turns on- `hello`, and std’s option logging
- `RUST_LOG=error,hello=warn`turn on global error logging and also warn for- `hello`
- `RUST_LOG=error,hello=off`turn on global error logging, but turn off logging for- `hello`
- `RUST_LOG=off`turns off all logging for the application
- `RUST_LOG=OFF`turns off all logging for the application (same as previous)

[§](https://docs.rs#filtering-results)Filtering results

A `RUST_LOG` directive may include a regex filter. The syntax is to append `/`
followed by a regex. Each message is checked against the regex, and is only
logged if it matches. Note that the matching is done after formatting the
log string but before adding any logging meta-data. There is a single filter
for all modules.

Some examples:

- `hello/foo`turns on all logging for the ‘hello’ module where the log message includes ‘foo’.
- `info/f.o`turns on all info logging where the log message includes ‘foo’, ‘f1o’, ‘fao’, etc.
- `hello=debug/foo*foo`turns on debug logging for ‘hello’ where the log message includes ‘foofoo’ or ‘fofoo’ or ‘fooooooofoo’, etc.
- `error,hello=warn/[0-9]scopes`turn on global error logging and also warn for hello. In both cases the log message must include a single digit number followed by ‘scopes’.

[§](https://docs.rs#capturing-logs-in-tests)Capturing logs in tests

Records logged during `cargo test` will not be captured by the test harness by default.
The [ Builder::is_test](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.is_test) method can be used in unit tests to ensure logs will be captured:

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use log::info;
    fn init() {
        let _ = env_logger::builder().is_test(true).try_init();
    }
    #[test]
    fn it_works() {
        init();
        info!("This record will be captured by `cargo test`");
        assert_eq!(2, 1 + 1);
    }
}
```
Enabling test capturing comes at the expense of color and other style support and may have performance implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#colors)Colors

Outputting of colors and other styles can be controlled by the `RUST_LOG_STYLE`
environment variable. It accepts the following [values](https://docs.rs/fmt/enum.WriteStyle.html):

- `auto`(default) will attempt to print style characters, but don’t force the issue. If the console isn’t available on Windows, or if TERM=dumb, for example, then don’t print colors.
- `always`will always print style characters even if they aren’t supported by the terminal. This includes emitting ANSI colors on Windows if the console API is unavailable.
- `never`will never print style characters.

Color may be applied in the logged message or a [custom formatter](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html).

Logging of untrusted inputs can cause unexpected behavior as they may include ANSI escape codes which will be forwarded to the users terminal as part of “Weaponizing ANSI Escape Sequences”.

Mitigations include:

- Setting `RUST_LOG_STYLE=never`to have all ANSI escape codes stripped
- In the application, calling `Builder::write_style(Never)`
- In the application, [stripping ANSI escape codes](https://docs.rs/anstream/latest/anstream/adapter/fn.strip_str.html)from user inputs

Note: deactivating the build-time feature `color` is not a mitigation as that removes all ANSI escape code
stripping from `env_logger`.

[§](https://docs.rs#tweaking-the-default-format)Tweaking the default format

Parts of the default format can be excluded from the log output using the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html).
The following example excludes the timestamp from the log output:

```
env_logger::builder()
    .format_timestamp(None)
    .init();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#stability-of-the-default-format)Stability of the default format

The default format won’t optimise for long-term stability, and explicitly makes no
guarantees about the stability of its output across major, minor or patch version
bumps during `0.x`.

If you want to capture or interpret the output of `env_logger` programmatically
then you should use a custom format.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-a-custom-format)Using a custom format

Custom formats can be provided as closures to the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html).
These closures take a

[and](https://docs.rs/fmt/struct.Formatter.html)

`Formatter``log::Record` as arguments:```
use std::io::Write;
env_logger::builder()
    .format(|buf, record| {
        writeln!(buf, "{}: {}", record.level(), record.args())
    })
    .init();
```
See the [ fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html) module for more details about custom formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#specifying-defaults-for-environment-variables)Specifying defaults for environment variables

`env_logger` can read configuration from environment variables.
If these variables aren’t present, the default value to use can be tweaked with the [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) type.
The following example defaults to log

`warn` and above if the `RUST_LOG` environment variable
isn’t set:```
use env_logger::Env;
env_logger::Builder::from_env(Env::default().default_filter_or("warn")).init();
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use self::fmt::`- [TimestampPrecision](https://docs.rs/fmt/enum.TimestampPrecision.html);
- `pub use self::fmt::`- [WriteStyle](https://docs.rs/fmt/enum.WriteStyle.html);

# similar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/similar/^2.1.0/

## Expand description

This crate implements diffing utilities. It attempts to provide an abstraction interface over different types of diffing algorithms. The design of the library is inspired by pijul’s diff library by Pierre-Étienne Meunier and also inherits the patience diff algorithm from there.

The API of the crate is split into high and low level functionality. Most of what you probably want to use is available top level. Additionally the following sub modules exist:

- `algorithms`
- `udiff`
- `utils`

[§](https://docs.rs#sequence-diffing)Sequence Diffing

If you want to diff sequences generally indexable things you can use the
[ capture_diff](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff.html) and

[functions. They will directly diff an indexable object or slice and return a vector of](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_slices.html)

`capture_diff_slices`[objects.](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffOp.html)

`DiffOp````
use similar::{Algorithm, capture_diff_slices};
let a = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let b = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 7];
let ops = capture_diff_slices(Algorithm::Myers, &a, &b);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#text-diffing)Text Diffing

Similar provides helpful utilities for text (and more specifically line) diff
operations.  The main type you want to work with is [ TextDiff](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html) which
uses the underlying diff algorithms to expose a convenient API to work with
texts:

```
use similar::{ChangeTag, TextDiff};
let diff = TextDiff::from_lines(
    "Hello World\nThis is the second line.\nThis is the third.",
    "Hallo Welt\nThis is the second line.\nThis is life.\nMoar and more",
);
for change in diff.iter_all_changes() {
    let sign = match change.tag() {
        ChangeTag::Delete => "-",
        ChangeTag::Insert => "+",
        ChangeTag::Equal => " ",
    };
    print!("{}{}", sign, change);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#trailing-newlines)Trailing Newlines

When working with line diffs (and unified diffs in general) there are two
“philosophies” to look at lines.  One is to diff lines without their newline
character, the other is to diff with the newline character.  Typically the
latter is done because text files do not *have* to end in a newline character.
As a result there is a difference between `foo\n` and `foo` as far as diffs
are concerned.

In similar this is handled on the [ Change](https://docs.rs/struct.Change.html) or

[level. If a diff was created via](https://docs.rs/struct.InlineChange.html)

`InlineChange`[the text diffing system is instructed to check if there are missing newlines encountered (](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.from_lines)

`TextDiff::from_lines`[returns true).](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.newline_terminated)

`TextDiff::newline_terminated`In any case the [ Change](https://docs.rs/struct.Change.html) object has a convenience method called

[which returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Change.html#method.missing_newline)

`Change::missing_newline``true` if the change is missing
a trailing newline.  Armed with that information the caller knows to handle
this by either rendering a virtual newline at that position or to indicate
it in different ways.  For instance the unified diff code will render the
special `\ No newline at end of file` marker.[§](https://docs.rs#bytes-vs-unicode)Bytes vs Unicode

Similar module concerns itself with a looser definition of “text” than you would
normally see in Rust.  While by default it can only operate on [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) types,
by enabling the

`bytes` feature it gains support for byte slices with some
caveats.A lot of text diff functionality assumes that what is being diffed constitutes text, but in the real world it can often be challenging to ensure that this is all valid utf-8. Because of this the crate is built so that most functionality also still works with bytes for as long as they are roughly ASCII compatible.

This means you will be successful in creating a unified diff from latin1 encoded bytes but if you try to do the same with EBCDIC encoded bytes you will only get garbage.

[§](https://docs.rs#ops-vs-changes)Ops vs Changes

Because very commonly two compared sequences will largely match this module splits its functionality into two layers:

Changes are encoded as [diff operations](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffOp.html).  These are
ranges of the differences by index in the source sequence.  Because this
can be cumbersome to work with, a separate method [ DiffOp::iter_changes](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffOp.html#method.iter_changes)
(and

[when working with text diffs) is provided which expands all the changes on an item by item level encoded in an operation.](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.iter_changes)

`TextDiff::iter_changes`As the [ TextDiff::grouped_ops](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html#method.grouped_ops) method can isolate clusters of changes
this even works for very long files if paired with this method.

[§](https://docs.rs#deadlines-and-performance)Deadlines and Performance

For large and very distinct inputs the algorithms as implemented can take
a very, very long time to execute.  Too long to make sense in practice.
To work around this issue all diffing algorithms also provide a version
that accepts a deadline which is the point in time as defined by an
[ Instant](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html) after which the algorithm should give up.  What giving up means
depends on the algorithm.  For instance due to the recursive, divide and
conquer nature of Myer’s diff you will still get a pretty decent diff in
many cases when a deadline is reached.  Whereas on the other hand the LCS
diff is unlikely to give any decent results in such a situation.

The [ TextDiff](https://docs.rs/struct.TextDiff.html) type also lets you configure a deadline and/or timeout
when performing a text diff.

Note that on wasm targets calling [ Instant::now](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html#method.now) will result in a panic
unless you enable the

`wasm32_web_time` feataure.  By default similar will
silently disable the deadline checks internally unless that feature is
enabled.[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

The crate by default does not have any dependencies however for some use cases it’s useful to pull in extra functionality. Likewise you can turn off some functionality.

- `text`: this feature is enabled by default and enables the text based diffing types such as- `TextDiff`
- `unicode`: when this feature is enabled the text diffing functionality gains the ability to diff on a grapheme instead of character level. This is particularly useful when working with text containing emojis. This pulls in some relatively complex dependencies for working with the unicode database.
- `bytes`: this feature adds support for working with byte slices in text APIs in addition to unicode strings. This pulls in the- `bstr`
- `inline`: this feature gives access to additional functionality of the text diffing to provide inline information about which values changed in a line diff. This currently also enables the- `unicode`feature.
- `serde`: this feature enables serialization to some types in this crate. For enums without payload deserialization is then also supported.
- `wasm32_web_time`: this feature swaps out the use of- `std::time`- `web_time`crate. Because this is a change to the public interface, this feature must be used with care. The instant type for this crate is then re-exported top-level module.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- The various iterators this crate provides.

- [utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff.html)- diff
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_deadline.html)- diff_ - deadline
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_slices.html)- diff_ - slices
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_diff_slices_deadline.html)- diff_ - slices_ - deadline
- Creates a diff between old and new with the given algorithm capturing the ops.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_close_matches.html)- close_ - matches
- Use the text differ to find `n`close matches.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_diff_ratio.html)- diff_ - ratio
- Return a measure of similarity in the range `0..=1`.
- [group_](https://docs.rs/fn.group_diff_ops.html)- diff_ - ops
- Isolate change clusters by eliminating ranges with no changes.

- Generates all the ISLE source files used in Cranelift from the meta-language.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_isle_for_assembler.html)🔒- isle_ - for_ - assembler
- Generate the ISLE definitions; this provides ISLE glue to access the
assembler instructions in [cranelift_assembler_x64_meta](https://docs.rs/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/0.133.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_assembler_x64_meta/index.html).
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_isle_for_shared_defs.html)🔒- isle_ - for_ - shared_ - defs
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_rust.html)- rust
- Generates all the Rust source files used in Cranelift from the meta-language.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_rust_for_shared_defs.html)🔒- rust_ - for_ - shared_ - defs
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_rust_macro_for_assembler.html)🔒- rust_ - macro_ - for_ - assembler
- Generate a macro containing builder functions for the assembler’s ISLE
constructors; this provides Rust implementations backing up the ISLE
definitions in [generate_isle_for_assembler](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_isle_for_assembler.html).
- [isa_](https://docs.rs/fn.isa_from_arch.html)- from_ - arch
- Generate an ISA from an architecture string (e.g. “x86_64”).

# cranelift_isle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-isle/=0.133.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#isle-instruction-selection--lowering-expressions)ISLE: Instruction Selection / Lowering Expressions

ISLE is a domain specific language (DSL) for instruction selection and lowering
clif instructions to vcode’s `MachInst`s in Cranelift.

ISLE is a statically-typed term-rewriting language. You define rewriting rules
that map input terms (clif instructions) into output terms (`MachInst`s). These
rules get compiled down into Rust source test that uses a tree of `match`
expressions as good as or better than what you would have written by hand.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- Abstract syntax tree (AST) created from parsed ISLE.
- [codegen](https://docs.rs/codegen/index.html)
- Generate Rust code from a series of Sequences.
- [compile](https://docs.rs/compile/index.html)
- Compilation process, from AST to Sema to Sequences of Insts.
- [disjointsets](https://docs.rs/disjointsets/index.html)
- Implementation of `DisjointSets`
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types.
- [files](https://docs.rs/files/index.html)
- [lexer](https://docs.rs/lexer/index.html)
- Lexer for the ISLE language.
- [overlap](https://docs.rs/overlap/index.html)
- Overlap detection for rules in ISLE.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Parser for ISLE language.
- [printer](https://docs.rs/printer/index.html)
- Printer for ISLE language.
- [recursion](https://docs.rs/recursion/index.html)
- Recursion checking for ISLE terms.
- [sema](https://docs.rs/sema/index.html)
- Semantic analysis.
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serialize/index.html)
- Put “sea of nodes” representation of a `RuleSet`into a sequential order.
- [stablemapset](https://docs.rs/stablemapset/index.html)
- Implementations of hashmap and hashset that asvoid observing non-determinism in iteration order. In a separate module so the compiler can prevent access to the internal implementation details.
- [trie_](https://docs.rs/trie_again/index.html)- again
- A strongly-normalizing intermediate representation for ISLE rules. This representation is chosen to closely reflect the operations we can implement in Rust, to make code generation easy.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [log](https://docs.rs/macro.log.html)
- Log a compiler-internal message for debugging purposes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Call](https://docs.rs/struct.CallInfo.html)- Info
- Out-of-line data for calls, to keep the size of `Inst`down.
- [Compile](https://docs.rs/struct.CompileError.html)- Error
- Compilation error, with the accompanying function to help printing it.
- [Context](https://docs.rs/struct.Context.html)
- Persistent data structures and compilation pipeline.
- [Final](https://docs.rs/struct.Final.html)
- Status of a compiled artifact ready to use.
- [Finalized](https://docs.rs/struct.FinalizedMachCallSite.html)- Mach - Call - Site
- A call site record resulting from a compilation.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameLayout.html)- Layout
- Structure describing the layout of a function’s stack frame.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBuffer.html)- Buffer
- A buffer of output to be produced, fixed up, and then emitted to a CodeSink in bulk.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBufferDebugTagList.html)- Buffer - Debug - TagList
- Iterator item for visiting debug tags.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBufferFinalized.html)- Buffer - Finalized
- A `MachBuffer`once emission is completed: holds generated code and records, without fixups. This allows the type to be independent of the backend.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBufferFrameLayout.html)- Buffer - Frame - Layout
- Stack-frame layout information carried through to machine code. This provides sufficient information to interpret an active stack frame from a running function, if provided.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachCallSite.html)- Call - Site
- A call site record resulting from a compilation.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachLabel.html)- Label
- A label refers to some offset in a `MachBuffer`. It may not be resolved at the point at which it is used by emitted code; the buffer records “fixups” for references to the label, and will come back and patch the code appropriately when the label’s location is eventually known.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachSrcLoc.html)- SrcLoc
- A source-location mapping resulting from a compilation.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachTextSectionBuilder.html)- Text - Section - Builder
- Implementation of the `TextSectionBuilder`trait backed by`MachBuffer`.
- [Mach](https://docs.rs/struct.MachTrap.html)- Trap
- A trap record resulting from a compilation.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenPatchRegion.html)- Patch - Region
- Represents the beginning of an editable region in the `MachBuffer``OpenPatchRegion``MachBuffer::end_patchable``OpenPatchRegion`
- [Patch](https://docs.rs/struct.PatchRegion.html)- Region
- A region in the `MachBuffer``MachBuffer::start_patchable``PatchRegion``MachBuffer::end_patchable``PatchRegion::patch`
- [RealReg](https://docs.rs/struct.RealReg.html)
- A real (physical) register. This corresponds to one of the target ISA’s named registers and can be used as an instruction operand.
- [Reg](https://docs.rs/struct.Reg.html)
- A register named in an instruction. This register can be a virtual
register, a fixed physical register, or a named spillslot (after
regalloc). It does not have any constraints applied to it: those
can be added later in `MachInst::get_operands()`when the`Reg`s are converted to`Operand`s.
- [Take](https://docs.rs/struct.TakeAndReplace.html)- AndReplace
- An RAII type to temporarily take a `U`out of a`T`and then put it back again on drop.
- [VCode](https://docs.rs/struct.VCodeConstant.html)- Constant
- A use of a constant by one or more VCode instructions; see [VCodeConstants](https://docs.rs/struct.VCodeConstants.html).
- [VCode](https://docs.rs/struct.VCodeConstants.html)- Constants
- This structure tracks the large constants used in VCode that will be emitted separately by the
[MachBuffer](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBuffer.html).
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueLocRange.html)- LocRange
- Value location range.
- [Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.Writable.html)
- A type wrapper that indicates a register type is writable. The
underlying register can be extracted, and the type wrapper can be
built using an arbitrary register. Hence, this type-level wrapper
is not strictly a guarantee. However, “casting” to a writable
register is an explicit operation for which we can
audit. Ordinarily, internal APIs in the compiler backend should
take a `Writable<Reg>`whenever the register is written, and the usual, frictionless way to get one of these is to allocate a new temporary.

# cranelift-codegen 0.133.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-codegen/0.133.0/features

# cranelift_bforest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-bforest/0.133.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_bforest/index.html

## Expand description

A forest of B+-trees.

This crate provides a data structures representing a set of small ordered sets or maps. It is implemented as a forest of B+-trees all allocating nodes out of the same pool.

**These are not general purpose data structures that are somehow magically faster that the
standard library’s  BTreeSet and BTreeMap types.**

The tradeoffs are different:

- Keys and values are expected to be small and copyable. We optimize for 32-bit types.
- A comparator object is used to compare keys, allowing smaller “context free” keys.
- Empty trees have a very small 32-bit footprint.
- All the trees in a forest can be cleared in constant time.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- B-tree mapping from `K`to`V`.
- [MapCursor](https://docs.rs/struct.MapCursor.html)
- A position in a `Map`used to navigate and modify the ordered map.
- [MapCursor](https://docs.rs/struct.MapCursorMut.html)- Mut
- A position in a `Map`used to navigate and modify the ordered map.
- [MapForest](https://docs.rs/struct.MapForest.html)
- Memory pool for a forest of `Map`instances.
- [MapInto](https://docs.rs/struct.MapIntoIter.html)- Iter
- A consuming iterator of a `Map`, yielding its key-value pairs.
- [MapIter](https://docs.rs/struct.MapIter.html)
- An iterator visiting the key-value pairs of a `Map`.
- [MapRange](https://docs.rs/struct.MapRange.html)
- An immutable iterator over a range of values, returned by `Map::range`.
- [Set](https://docs.rs/struct.Set.html)
- B-tree representing an ordered set of `K`s using`C`for comparing elements.
- [SetCursor](https://docs.rs/struct.SetCursor.html)
- A position in a `Set`used to navigate and modify the ordered set.
- [SetForest](https://docs.rs/struct.SetForest.html)
- Memory pool for a forest of `Set`instances.
- [SetIter](https://docs.rs/struct.SetIter.html)
- An iterator visiting the elements of a `Set`.

- Key comparator.

# cranelift_control - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-control/0.133.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_control/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cranelift-control)Cranelift Control

This is the home of the control plane of chaos mode, a compilation feature
intended to be turned on for certain fuzz targets. When the feature is
turned off, as is normally the case, [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) will be a zero-sized
type and optimized away.

While the feature is turned on, the struct [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)
provides functionality to tap into pseudo-randomness at specific locations
in the code. It may be used for targeted fuzzing of compiler internals,
e.g. manipulate heuristic optimizations, clobber undefined register bits
etc.

There are two ways to acquire a [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html):

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary)for the real deal (requires the- `fuzz`feature, enabled by default)
- [default](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.default)for an “empty” control plane which always returns default values

[§](https://docs.rs#fuel-limit)Fuel Limit

Controls the number of mutations or optimizations that the compiler will perform before stopping.

When a perturbation introduced by chaos mode triggers a bug, it may not be immediately clear which of the introduced perturbations was the trigger. The fuel limit can then be used to binary-search for the trigger. It limits the number of perturbations introduced by the control plane. The fuel limit will typically be set with a command line argument passed to a fuzz target. For example:

`cargo fuzz run --features chaos $TARGET -- --fuel=16`[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-support)`no_std` support

This crate compiles in `no_std` environments, although both the `fuzz`
or `chaos` features have a dependency on `std`. This means that on `no_std`
you can’t use [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary) to initialize [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) and can’t enable
chaos mode, although the rest of the usual [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) API is available.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)- Plane
- A shim for ControlPlane when chaos mode is disabled.
Please see the [crate-level documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html).

---

# cranelift_entity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/0.133.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_entity/index.html

## Expand description

Array-based data structures using densely numbered entity references as mapping keys.

This crate defines a number of data structures based on arrays. The arrays are not indexed by
`usize` as usual, but by *entity references* which are integers wrapped in new-types. This has
a couple advantages:

- Improved type safety. The various map and set types accept a specific key type, so there is no confusion about the meaning of an array index, as there is with plain arrays.
- Smaller indexes. The normal `usize`index is often 64 bits which is way too large for most purposes. The entity reference types can be smaller, allowing for more compact data structures.

The `EntityRef` trait should be implemented by types to be used as indexed. The `entity_impl!`
macro provides convenient defaults for types wrapping `u32` which is common.

- `PrimaryMap`
- `SecondaryMap`
- `SparseMap`
- `EntitySet`
- `EntityList`- `Vec`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [packed_](https://docs.rs/packed_option/index.html)- option
- Compact representation of `Option<T>`for types with a reserved value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Macro which provides the common implementation of a 32-bit entity reference.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Entity](https://docs.rs/struct.EntityList.html)- List
- A small list of entity references allocated from a pool.

- A set of `K`for densely indexed entity references.

- Iterate over all keys in order.
- [Keys](https://docs.rs/struct.Keys.html)

- [Primary](https://docs.rs/struct.PrimaryMap.html)- Map

- [Secondary](https://docs.rs/struct.SecondaryMap.html)- Map

- An iterator over the elements in an `EntitySet`.
- [Sparse](https://docs.rs/struct.SparseMap.html)- Map
- A sparse mapping of entity references.

# gimli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gimli/0.33.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gimli/index.html

## Expand description

`gimli` is a library for reading and writing the
[DWARF debugging format](https://dwarfstd.org/).

See the [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) and [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) modules
for examples and API documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

Cargo features that can be enabled with `gimli`:

-
`std`: Enabled by default. Use the`std`library. Disabling this feature allows using`gimli`in embedded environments that do not have access to`std`.
-
`read`: Enabled by default. Enables the`read`module. Use of`std`is optional. Requires the`alloc`crate.
-
`read-core`: Enabled by default. Enables a subset of the`read`module that does not require the`alloc`crate.
-
`endian-reader`: Enabled by default. Enables the`EndianReader``stable_deref_trait`crate.
-
`write`: Enabled by default. Enables the`write`module. Use of`std`is optional. Requires the`alloc`crate. Enabling both`read`and`write`will also enable conversion functionality in the`write`module.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [constants](https://docs.rs/constants/index.html)
- Constant definitions.
- [leb128](https://docs.rs/leb128/index.html)
- Read and write DWARF’s “Little Endian Base 128” (LEB128) variable length integer encoding.
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Read DWARF debugging information.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clone](https://docs.rs/trait.CloneStableDeref.html)- Stable - Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types where clones deref to the same address. This has all the requirements of StableDeref, and additionally requires that after calling clone(), both the old and new value deref to the same address. For example, Rc and Arc implement CloneStableDeref, but Box and Vec do not.
- [Endianity](https://docs.rs/trait.Endianity.html)
- A trait describing the endianity of some buffer.
- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableDeref.html)- Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types that deref to a stable address, even when moved. For example, this is implemented by Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String, among others. Even when a Box is moved, the underlying storage remains at a fixed location.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [case_](https://docs.rs/fn.case_folding_djb_hash.html)- folding_ - djb_ - hash
- Calculate a case folding DJB hash for the DWARF name index.

# FrameLayout in cranelift_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/=0.133.0/struct.FrameLayout.html

```
pub struct FrameLayout {
    pub word_bytes:
```
[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub incoming_args_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub tail_args_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub setup_area_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub clobber_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub fixed_frame_storage_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub stackslots_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub outgoing_args_size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub clobbered_callee_saves: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.Writable.html)<[RealReg](https://docs.rs/struct.RealReg.html)>>,
    pub function_calls: FunctionCalls,
}## Expand description

Structure describing the layout of a function’s stack frame.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.word_bytes)

`word_bytes: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Word size in bytes, so this struct can be
monomorphic/independent of `ABIMachineSpec`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.incoming_args_size)

`incoming_args_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)N.B. The areas whose sizes are given in this structure fully cover the current function’s stack frame, from high to low stack addresses in the sequence below. Each size contains any alignment padding that may be required by the ABI. Size of incoming arguments on the stack. This is not technically part of this function’s frame, but code in the function will still need to access it. Depending on the ABI, we may need to set up a frame pointer to do so; we also may need to pop this area from the stack upon return.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.tail_args_size)

`tail_args_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)The size of the incoming argument area, taking into account any
potential increase in size required for tail calls present in the
function. In the case that no tail calls are present, this value
will be the same as [ Self::incoming_args_size](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameLayout.html#structfield.incoming_args_size).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.setup_area_size)

`setup_area_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Size of the “setup area”, typically holding the return address and/or the saved frame pointer. This may be written either during the call itself (e.g. a pushed return address) or by code emitted from gen_prologue_frame_setup. In any case, after that code has completed execution, the stack pointer is expected to point to the bottom of this area. The same holds at the start of code emitted by gen_epilogue_frame_restore.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.clobber_size)

`clobber_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Size of the area used to save callee-saved clobbered registers. This area is accessed by code emitted from gen_clobber_save and gen_clobber_restore.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.fixed_frame_storage_size)

`fixed_frame_storage_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Storage allocated for the fixed part of the stack frame. This contains stack slots and spill slots.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.stackslots_size)

`stackslots_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)The size of all stackslots.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.outgoing_args_size)

`outgoing_args_size: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Stack size to be reserved for outgoing arguments, if used by the current ABI, or 0 otherwise. After gen_clobber_save and before gen_clobber_restore, the stack pointer points to the bottom of this area.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.clobbered_callee_saves)

`clobbered_callee_saves: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.Writable.html)<[RealReg](https://docs.rs/struct.RealReg.html)>>Sorted list of callee-saved registers that are clobbered according to the ABI. These registers will be saved and restored by gen_clobber_save and gen_clobber_restore.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.function_calls)

`function_calls: FunctionCalls`The function’s call pattern classification.
